activity: to explain how nicotine causes addiction in the brain's reward pathway
knowledge_domain: to explain how nicotine causes addiction in the brain's reward pathway
fact: Nicotine causes brain cells in the reward pathway to release dopamine, a chemical messenger linked to pleasure and motivation.
story:
The automatic doors of the pharmacy whooshed open, and Raphael rushed in so fast he nearly knocked over a display of vitamins. He had exactly one hour before his health presentation, and his poster still had a giant blank space where the most important sentence should go.

"Why are we even here?" Marek asked, drifting toward the candy aisle. "Your topic is brains, not bandages." Marek's actual plan for the afternoon involved convincing the cashier that sour worms counted as a nutritious snack, a project he had been working on for weeks.

"Grandpa's here picking up his patches," Raphael said. "He smoked for twenty years and quit, and I never asked him why it was hard. He's like a primary source." He spotted his grandfather at the counter, patting his pockets for his wallet, and jogged over. "Grandpa. Quick question. When you smoked, what did it actually feel like?"

His grandfather chuckled. "Felt like a little reward. Like your brain patting you on the back. Then the patting stopped, and you wanted another cigarette to get it back." He paid for his patches and tucked the bag under his arm.

Raphael pulled out his phone and typed fast. At school they had learned the word dopamine, and now the pieces started fitting together in his head like a puzzle snapping into place. Nicotine must be tricking the brain cells in the reward pathway, making them release dopamine, and dopamine was a chemical messenger tied to pleasure and motivation. That was the whole loop. The brain got a pat on the back from a chemical, and it kept asking for another one. He looked up. "So your brain wasn't weak, it was getting fooled by chemistry." His grandfather nodded slowly, like Raphael had said something worth keeping.

"Hey, science boy," Marek called from aisle three, holding up a bag of sour worms and a bottle of vitamins. "If I buy the vitamins too, that's balanced, right? Like lichen. Lichen is a partnership. My mom showed me a rock covered in it." The cashier raised one eyebrow and did not emit a single word of agreement, which Marek took as a maybe.

Outside, Raphael read his note out loud one more time, bouncing on his heels. "Nicotine makes brain cells in the reward pathway release dopamine, a chemical messenger linked to pleasure and motivation. That's my whole blank space filled." He held the phone up to the sky like a trophy. Marek tore open the sour worms with his teeth. "Presentations are boring," he said, chewing. "Mine's about why my dog barks at the vacuum. But fine, yours is good too." Raphael grinned and ran for the bus.

activity: going to a first school dance
knowledge_domain: going to a first school dance
fact: A glow stick shines brighter but runs out faster when it is warm, and glows dimmer but lasts longer when it is cold.
story:
Brielle stood in the school parking lot behind her mom's car, holding two glow sticks and frowning at them. She had bought a pack of eight at the party store that afternoon, cracked them all at once so they'd be ready, and left them on the dashboard while she changed into her dress. The car had sat in the sun the whole time.

The two sticks in her hand blazed like small green flares, brighter than any glow stick she could remember. That was the good news. The bad news was that an hour ago they had been even brighter, and she could see the difference. She cracked a fresh one from the pack she had kept in her pocket and compared them side by side. The pocket one came up dim, almost vague in its green, like someone had watered down the color. The dashboard ones were still winning, but fading fast, and the dance had not even started.

"Are those dying already?" Anabel asked, coming across the parking lot with Delaney. Both of them wore paper crowns from the dance committee, which had run out of anything better.

"They're brighter than yours," Brielle said, "but they were brighter than this twenty minutes ago. Mine from my pocket are dimmer, but they haven't changed at all since I cracked them."

Delaney held up her own stick, a blue one she had been carrying in her purse. "Mine's medium. I don't get it."

"It's the heat," Brielle said slowly. "The dashboard was cooking mine all afternoon. Yours were somewhere in between." She looked at her mom's car, then at the cooler some eighth graders had set up by the gym doors for sodas. She walked over, opened it, and dropped her two blazing sticks into the ice water between the juice boxes. "If warm makes them bright and fast, maybe cold makes them slow. I want to see what happens when they cool down."

"Is that how it works?" Anabel asked.

"I think so. Warm ones shine brighter but run out faster. Cold ones glow dimmer but last longer. Watch, I'll test it." She set a timer on her phone for fifteen minutes and followed the others toward the gym.

The gym had a fog machine, a playlist full of songs the students all claimed to hate and danced to anyway, and folding tables along one wall. Ms. Nwosu, who was supervising the door, confiscated somebody's air horn within the first ten minutes, which everyone agreed was the right call. Brielle danced with Anabel and Delaney, kept checking her phone, and thought about the irony of the situation: the sticks she had pampered on the dashboard, the ones she had wanted to be her best, were the ones burning through their glow before the party even began, while the neglected pocket sticks just kept going.

When the timer went off she slipped back outside. The two dashboard sticks were still in the ice water, floating between the juice boxes, and when she lifted one out it had gone dim, dimmer than her pocket stick had ever been. She cracked a fresh stick, held it over the ice water in her cupped hand so the cold would reach it, and waited. The new stick stayed faint, almost nothing, a thin green line in the dark. She put it back in the cold, zipped it into her jacket pocket against the ice, and carried it back inside, where it went on glowing, faint and stubborn, all the way to the last song.

Afterward, in the parking lot waiting for rides, Delaney peered at it. "It's still going. Barely, but it's going."

"That's the whole point," Brielle said. "Slow and dim beats bright and dead." She turned the thin green line over in her fingers. "I'm putting mine in the freezer tonight. If it's still glowing at breakfast, I win."

"Win what?" Delaney asked.

"Nothing. Everything," Brielle said, and held it up to the streetlight.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: A 2018 study by Jeffrey Hall of the University of Kansas found it takes about 50 hours together to turn an acquaintance into a casual friend.
story:
Cooper found the number in a library book about friendship while packing his room into boxes. A 2018 study by Jeffrey Hall of the University of Kansas said it takes about 50 hours together to turn an acquaintance into a casual friend. He read the page twice, then dug a notebook out of a half-taped box and wrote it down. Fifty hours. Was that how much he had with Jazmine and Deklan? Or had they already spent it, years ago, back when nobody was counting?

"Are you seriously doing math during a goodbye party?" Deklan stood in the doorway holding a pizza box. Jazmine pushed past him with the root beer. It was their last afternoon together, because the moving truck came tomorrow.

Cooper turned the notebook around so they could see his columns. Every lunch, every soccer practice, every Saturday at the creek. He'd been estimating all week. "I think you two are past fifty hours each. Like way past. But here's what irritates me. If we made new friends the same way, it should take the same amount of time again. New kids, fifty hours. That's more than six full school days of just... being together."

Jazmine frowned at the columns. "That seems long. One good lunch should do it." She had a reputation for deciding things fast, whether it was a pizza topping or a person, and the whole class knew it.

"That's what I thought too," Cooper said. "So I tested it. Remember Marcus, from science camp? We had one amazing day, the ropes course, and I figured we were friends after that. I messaged him in October. He never wrote back." Deklan laughed so hard he almost dropped the pizza, and Cooper had to admit the evidence was brutal. One lunch, even a great one, apparently wasn't fifty hours.

Jazmine sat on a box marked BOOKS and stared at the numbers for a long moment. "Okay," she said slowly. "So the kid who sits near you at lunch in the new town. You can't rush it." Cooper nodded. It was strange and a little wonderful, like finding a hidden rule inside something he'd always thought just happened. They voted on the last slice, and it was unanimous: Deklan got it, since he'd carried the box. Then Jazmine grabbed Cooper's notebook and wrote on the back cover, HOUR 1 STARTS WHEN YOU GET THERE.

"Take it," Cooper said. "Start counting for me too."

activity: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
knowledge_domain: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
fact: Cutting an onion in half from top to root and laying each half flat side down gives a steady base, so the onion cannot roll while you slice it.
story:
Aiden had signed up for the school's cooking club before it filled, but then the first two sessions were cancelled, so his mother suggested he practice at home instead. "You wanted to make sauce from scratch," she said, handing him three onions and a sharp knife. "Start there." He set the cutting board on the counter and peeled the first onion, which immediately rolled away from his blade and nearly tumbled onto the floor. He chased it with the flat of the knife and tried again, curling his fingers into the claw grip the club handout had shown, fingertips tucked under, knuckles forward. The onion rolled anyway.

He stopped and stared at it. The problem, he decided after a quick mental analysis, was that the onion was round and the board was smooth, so there was nothing holding it still. Maybe if he cut it in half first, each piece would sit better than the whole thing had. He lined the knife up from the top, the pointy end, down toward the root, and pressed straight through. The two halves fell open. He laid one half flat side down, and it sat there like it had been glued to the board. When he pushed the knife through it, the half did not budge at all.

"London, guess what," he said, balancing his phone against the flour jar with one onion-scented hand. "Cutting an onion in half from top to root and laying each half flat side down gives you a steady base, so it cannot roll while you slice it." He angled the camera so she could watch him run the knife through the second half in slow, even cuts, the layers coming apart like pages.

"That's actually satisfying," London's voice said from the speaker. "Show the claw again." He tucked his fingertips under and let his knuckles ride ahead of the blade, slicing half-moons into a ridge of pale curls. His eyes were streaming, but he kept going, because the sauce was not going to chop itself.

He warmed olive oil in the big pan, slid in the onions, and stirred while they softened. The change was gradual, from sharp white to translucent gold, and the smell shifted from stinging to sweet. He crushed a can of tomatoes with his hands, added salt, and let everything bubble while he boiled the pasta. From next door, Ms. Mercado called over the fence, "Whatever that is, save me a bowl."

Aiden tasted the sauce, added a pinch more salt, and ladled a generous portion into a container with a lid. He carried it straight to the fence.

activity: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
knowledge_domain: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
fact: When a variable appears on both sides, as in 5x + 2 = 3x + 10, subtracting 3x from both sides gathers the variable on one side: 2x + 2 = 10.
story:
Zoe slid her math worksheet across the library table and glared at it. "Problem seven is broken," she announced. "There's an x on both sides. 5x + 2 = 3x + 10. Which x am I supposed to move first?"

Fernando looked up from his book about sharks. "Maybe the left one. Left is first, like reading."

"That is not a legitimate math rule," Zoe said. "You just made that up out of reading."

"Sharks don't read," Fernando said serenely, and turned a page.

Ms. Park, shelving books two aisles over, gave them the look she gave kids who confused the returns cart with a book cart. Zoe ignored it and bent over the problem. Her intuition said there had to be a way to get the x's together, the way you get all the library books about sharks onto one shelf. But she couldn't see the answer hidden inside the equation. She could only see the equation itself.

"So infer," she muttered. "If the two sides are equal, then whatever I do to one side, I do to the other, and they stay equal. Like a seesaw." She tried it. Subtract 3x from the left side. Then, to keep the seesaw balanced, subtract 3x from the right side too. The 3x on the left vanished, and the 3x on the right vanished. What remained was 2x + 2 = 10. All the x's had gathered on the left, just like shark books on one shelf.

"Fernando. FERNANDO. It worked."

He peeked at her page. "You moved the right x first. Traitor."

"Wait." Zoe frowned. "Would it work the other way too? Subtracting 5x from both sides?"

"You already solved it. Don't wreck it."

She did it anyway. Minus 5x on each side gave 2 = 10 - 2x, and after a little more seesawing she got x = 4, the same answer as before. Zoe sat back so fast her chair squeaked. Either way worked. You could move whichever x you liked, and the answer came out the same, like walking to school by the park or by the creek.

Then Fernando leaned over, plucked the worksheet from under her hand, and wrote his name at the top.

"Hey!"

"I helped," he said. "Shark moral support is still support."

Ms. Park appeared beside them with the returns cart. "Fernando," she said, "write your name on your own work, or I'll shelve you in fiction."

"Which aisle?" Fernando asked hopefully.

"The one with the Very Serious Books About Sharks."

activity: going away to summer camp for the first time
knowledge_domain: going away to summer camp for the first time
fact: Dermatologists advise reapplying sunscreen about every two hours outdoors, and right after swimming or heavy sweating, because it wears and washes off.
story:
Felix had never been away from home for a whole week before, and he had decided the way to survive it was to treat camp like a science experiment. On the first night, the boys in his cabin gathered around the campfire while Mr. Kelly toasted marshmallows and handed out sticks. Felix pulled out a small notebook and announced that he was taking a census of the fire: who liked their marshmallows golden, who liked them burnt to a crisp, who refused to eat them at all. Malcom, who was in the bunk next to his, said the whole idea was ridiculous, and then waited politely to be counted first.

The next morning the whole cabin slathered on sunscreen before breakfast, because the schedule said LAKE DAY in big letters on the mess hall door. Felix was careful, covering his nose and the backs of his ears, which his mother always insisted on. Then they spent the whole afternoon in and out of the water, diving off the dock, racing to the raft, sweating on the sand between swims. Nobody mentioned sunscreen again.

At the evening campfire, Malcom sat hunched with his arms crossed over his chest, and when Felix leaned close he could see the red patches on Malcom's shoulders glowing even in the firelight. "I put it on this morning," Malcom said, wincing as he shifted on the log. "Same as you. How come you're fine and I look like a lobster?"

Felix didn't answer right away. He stared into the fire, watching the opaque black smoke curl up past the sparks, and tried to categorize everything that had happened since morning. Both of them had put on sunscreen. Both had been outside the same number of hours. Both had swum. The difference had to be hidden somewhere in all that, and he went through the day piece by piece like checking answers on a math test. Then he remembered something his older cousin had grumbled about last summer at the beach, something about sunscreen wearing off and washing off if you didn't keep putting it on. He grabbed his notebook and flipped to a blank page. "It comes off," Felix said slowly. "That's it. It doesn't last the whole day. If you're outside you have to put it on again about every two hours, and right after swimming, because water and sweat rinse it away." Malcom groaned. "We swam six times."

"So we needed it six more times," Felix said. "Plus the two-hour thing." He wrote it all down in capital letters and underlined it twice.

The next morning was another lake day, and Felix set the alarm on his watch. At the dock he stood with the bottle held high like a referee announcing a call. "Census time. Who's dry, who swam, and who's past two hours?" Malcom was first in line, and he didn't call it ridiculous at all. By afternoon, Malcom's shoulders still stung from yesterday, but they weren't any redder, and when Mr. Kelly wandered over to see what the line was for, Malcom held up the bottle and said, "Every two hours. Right after swimming. Pass it on."

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: In the Dutch Republic, prices for rare tulip bulbs soared in the winter of 1636 to 1637 and then collapsed in February 1637, when buyers stopped showing up.
story:
The trading cards had taken over Maplewood Middle School by October, and by November they had taken over the gas station too. Cole stood by the slushy machine watching Crosby wave a shiny Dragoon Titan card at the cashier, who shook his head. "Sixty dollars," the cashier said, pointing at the glass case where he kept the rare ones. "You want it, that's the price." Cole knew the same card had cost twenty in September, when everybody had one. Now nobody had one, because everybody wanted one.

"Tell you what," Crosby said to Cole outside, breath steaming in the cold. "I'll sell you my Voltback for forty. That's a deal. Next month it'll be eighty." Cole looked at the card. It was nice. It was not forty dollars nice, but he had forty dollars, and if prices only went up, waiting was losing. He pulled out the money, and then Eleanor came around the pump island with her bike, and something about her face made him pause.

"Nobody's trading at lunch anymore," she said. "Monday the whole sixth grade was fighting over cards. Today they were playing wall ball." She shrugged. "Except Bao still wants my Voltback." Cole's hand stayed in his pocket. Prices went up because lots of people wanted something there wasn't much of, that much he understood. But what happened when the wanting itself stopped?

Ms. Munro pulled up to the pump in her little green car, and while it filled she listened to Crosby argue that card prices only ever rose. "Sounds like the Dutch Republic," she said, stamping her feet against the cold. "Rare tulip bulb prices soared there in the winter of 1636 to 1637. Then in February 1637 the whole thing collapsed, because buyers stopped showing up." She capped her tank and smiled. "Look it up if you want to cite me."

Cole didn't buy the card. It nearly killed him not to. For three days he watched, and the watching was the test: if wanting was contagious like a sneeze spreading through a classroom, it could fade the same way. At the gas station on Saturday, the cashier had moved the cards to a bottom shelf. "Twenty bucks for the Titan now," he admitted. "Some kind of fungus got into the slushy mix and I need the case for the good cups." Crosby, standing beside him, made a small wounded noise. Eleanor arrived on her bike, held up her Voltback, and looked at Bao, who had followed her the whole way.

"Ten dollars," Bao said hopefully. Eleanor grinned and held up two fingers. "Twenty. Take it or I'll frame it," she said.

activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
knowledge_domain: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
fact: Article 1 of Germany's Basic Law, its constitution since 1949, begins with the words 'Human dignity shall be inviolable.'
story:
Keira had signed up for the community centre's Saturday civics club mostly because Jace dared her to, and now she regretted it, because Ms. Nakamura had just written ASSIGNMENT on the whiteboard and underneath it: explain one right from a constitution in your own words.

"I'll trade you," Jace whispered. "You do my paragraph, I'll conquer the vending machine for both of us."

"Everything in it is broken," Keira whispered back.

"That's the challenge."

Kaia leaned across the table. "My cousins live in Germany. I texted them last night because I was stuck too. They said their constitution doesn't even start with rights to vote or own stuff. It starts with something weirder."

"What, like a secret code?" Jace said.

Kaia checked her phone. "They sent me a picture of the page. Article 1. It says 'Human dignity shall be inviolable.'" She pronounced the last word slowly, careful of every syllable. "Germany's had that since 1949. It's called the Basic Law."

"Inviolable," Keira repeated. The word sat in her mouth like a stone she couldn't crack. She copied it into her notebook anyway.

Ms. Nakamura walked past. "Ten minutes until you present. One right, your own words, no reading off the page."

Keira stared at her notebook. The problem was that dignity wasn't a thing you could photograph or hold, like a jury summons or a driver's licence. How were you supposed to explain something invisible? She thought about the vending machine, of all things, how Jace assumed he could beat it, and how a person couldn't just be beaten on, either, because that was exactly what the rule forbade.

She tried an experiment. She wrote "Dignity means nobody gets to treat you like a thing" and held it up for Kaia. "Does that work?"

"Read it out loud," Kaia said.

Keira did, quietly, and then louder when both of them nodded. It did work, she realized, because a machine is a thing you kick and shake and use, and a person isn't, ever, and a constitution that starts by saying so is starting with the whole point.

When Ms. Nakamura called her name, Keira stood up so fast her chair scraped. "Germany's constitution is called the Basic Law, and Article 1, right at the top, says 'Human dignity shall be inviolable.'" She took a breath. "In my own words: every person matters in a way nobody is allowed to touch, not the government, not anyone. That comes first, before anything else."

Ms. Nakamura wrote something on her clipboard, and Jace slammed his fist against the vending machine in the corner, and the candy bar dropped.

activity: to explain how the Treaty of Versailles helped lead to the Second World War
knowledge_domain: to explain how the Treaty of Versailles helped lead to the Second World War
fact: The Treaty of Versailles forbade Germany to unite with Austria, but in March 1938 Hitler annexed Austria, an event called the Anschluss.
story:
Willow stood at the edge of the war memorial with her history project clutched against her jacket. The stone arch bore names of soldiers from her town, and on Monday she had to explain, out loud, how the Treaty of Versailles helped lead to the Second World War. The assignment intimidated her more than any math test ever had, because she could not see causes. A treaty was just paper. How was she supposed to show paper doing anything?

Ewan and Aliyah trailed up the path behind her, arguing about whose turn it was to carry the poster. "It's your poster," Aliyah said. "You made it crooked, you carry it." Ewan held it up. "It's not crooked, it's historical." The maps he had drawn showed Europe in 1920 and Europe in 1938, side by side, and Willow noticed for the tenth time that they did not match.

"Wait," she said, spreading both maps on the flat base of the memorial. "Where did Austria go?" She traced the smaller map with her finger. "It's right here in 1920. Then in 1938 there's just Germany, bigger." Ewan leaned over and squinted. "Maybe I drew it wrong." Willow checked her notes. "You didn't. The treaty said Germany couldn't unite with Austria. Then in March 1938 Hitler just annexed Austria anyway. There's even a word for it." Aliyah read from the notes. "It's called the Anschluss." She pronounced it three different ways before settling on one, and Ewan said his way was better, which started another argument that Willow ended by dropping a marker on Ewan's boot.

"Okay, but that's the thing," Willow said slowly. "This is how I show the paper doing something. The rules said no, and he did it anyway, and the map changed. That's like leaving a door open." She tried explaining it to a pigeon that had landed near the names on the arch, as practice. "A rule that everyone agrees to can still break, and when it breaks, you can see it on a map." The pigeon did not look convinced, but Aliyah did.

Mr. Dang, the neighbour who walked his dog past the memorial every afternoon, stopped and listened to her whole practice run. When she finished, he nodded at the carved names. "Some of those people were refugees who came here after that war," he said quietly. "Anger can be corrosive. It eats through everything." Willow thought about that, then wrote one last line at the bottom of her poster, while Ewan finally picked up the crooked thing and held it steady for her.

"There," she said. "Now the pigeon gets it too."

activity: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
knowledge_domain: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
fact: The piano's full name is pianoforte, meaning soft-loud, because the player can make notes soft or loud by how hard the keys are struck.
story:
Ethan slid onto the piano bench in Mr. Francis's studio and set his sheet music on the stand, but he didn't open it. Instead he stared at the row of black and white keys like they had cheated him.

"Same spot again?" Mr. Francis asked, settling into his chair by the window, where a bee was working the flowers on the sill, hopping from blossom to blossom to pollinate each one before moving on.

"Measure thirty-two," Ethan said. "I play it right and it still sounds wrong." He put his hands in position and played the passage, every note exact, every rhythm steady. It came out flat as a sidewalk.

Mr. Francis hummed a bar of it back, loud where Ethan had been quiet, then suddenly soft. "Hear the difference?"

"That's what the dynamics are for, I know. Piano, forte, crescendo. I can read them." Ethan tapped the markings on the page. "But when I try to play soft, I just play slow. When I try to play loud, I speed up. It's like my hands can't do one without the other."

Janelle, waiting on the bench by the door for her own lesson, looked up from her phone. "Mine does that too. I figured it was just a beginner thing."

"It's not a beginner thing," Ethan said slowly. He was remembering something from the very first lesson, months ago, when Mr. Francis had said the instrument's whole name out loud while polishing the fallboard. "Pianoforte," he said. "That's the full name. It means soft-loud, because the player can make notes soft or loud by how hard the keys are struck."

Mr. Francis smiled but said nothing, which was his way of saying continue.

"So it's not two separate controls," Ethan went on. "Loud isn't a pedal or a switch. It's how hard I hit the key. And if I'm hitting harder because I'm trying to be louder, maybe my whole arm tenses up, and tense arms rush." He looked down at his hands. "That's why the loud parts always run away from me."

"Test it," Mr. Francis said.

Ethan played measure thirty-two again. This time, at the forte, he imagined only his fingertips dropping from a greater height, his wrist staying loose. The notes came out strong and robust, filling the small room, but the tempo held steady, like a heartbeat that hadn't been startled.

Janelle sat forward. "Do it again but the other way. The soft part."

He played the piano section, easing his fingers down gently, letting his arm stay heavy and calm. It was quiet without being slow. For the first time, the passage sounded like weather changing instead of a machine changing gears.

Outside the window, the bee had finished with the sill flowers and drifted toward the garden, where an old log sat rotting under the ferns, some decomposer quietly turning it back to soil, unhurried, doing its work at exactly its own pace.

Ethan played the whole page through, forte and piano and back again, and when he finished, his hands were still relaxed in his lap. He thought about how, last week, he'd almost quit the piece entirely and told his mom the piano was a waste of money. He hadn't told Mr. Francis that. He wasn't sure he would.

"So it was never about reading the markings," Janelle said, standing and gathering her books as her turn came. "It was about the striking."

"That's one thing I got right today," Ethan said, and closed the lid gently, soft as the softest note he owned.

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: PolitiFact, a US fact-checking website founded in 2007, rates claims on a scale it calls the Truth-O-Meter, from True to Pants on Fire.
story:
The commercial blared from the kitchen TV just as Noemie set her poster board on Magalie's table. A voice declared that a candidate for governor had raised taxes eleven times, and Magalie's grandfather muttered, "That man is a liar, plain and simple." Magalie grabbed the remote and turned the volume up. "We could use this for our project," she said. "Mr. Yoon wants an example of a claim by tomorrow, and this one is perfect."

Noemie wrote the claim on a sticky note while Magalie's grandfather insisted it was true because he had read it somewhere. Noemie didn't want to assume he was wrong any more than she wanted to assume he was right. "We can look it up," she said. "If it's a checkable fact, someone has probably checked it already." Magalie pulled her laptop over, and the two of them crowded around the screen with the clock on the wall showing 7:40. Magalie's mother had said she would drive Noemie home at eight, so they had twenty minutes.

Magalie typed the candidate's name and the word "taxes." The first result was a website called PolitiFact. "It's a fact-checking website from the US," Noemie read off the About page, "founded in 2007." The site rated claims on a scale called the Truth-O-Meter, with levels that ran from True all the way down to a level named Pants on Fire. Noemie read that line twice. "Pants on Fire," she repeated. "That's what they call their lowest rating."

They found the exact claim from the commercial, word for word, in the site's archive. The Truth-O-Meter graphic beside it showed a rating in the middle of the scale, and the article explained what the candidate had actually voted for. "So it's not True, and it's not Pants on Fire," Magalie said. "It's somewhere in between." Noemie copied the rating onto the sticky note. "Grandpa said it was a flat-out lie," Magalie called toward the kitchen. "The fact-checkers disagree with you a little, Grandpa."

"It's an opinion that it's a lie," Noemie said, printing the page. "The claim itself is a fact you can check. That's the difference." She pasted the printout onto the poster board beside the sticky note, then added a section titled "Opinion vs. Claim." Magalie wrote the words "Truth-O-Meter, True to Pants on Fire" under the heading and drew a little meter with a needle pointing sideways.

From the kitchen doorway, her grandfather watched them work, arms folded. "So which is it, True or Pants on Fire?" he asked. Noemie tapped the poster. "Read the meter," she said.

activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
knowledge_domain: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
fact: The First Amendment to the US Constitution protects freedom of religion, speech, the press, peaceful assembly and petitioning the government.
story:
Alexis pressed her notebook against her chest and counted the marble steps of the courthouse, because counting kept her hands from shaking. Her civics class had been assigned to sit in on a public session and then explain one right from the constitution in her own words, and Mr. Gill had made it worse by promising to pick presenters at random. She had prepared for the Fifth Amendment, mostly because Vladimir kept calling it "the don't-snitch amendment," and she had practiced her explanation twice on the bus.

Inside, the hallway smelled like floor polish and old paper. Vladimir leaned against a radiator, juggling a pencil and trying to look calm, while Marc-Antoine paced and muttered about wanting to be called on first so he could "get it over with and win." He wanted the prize, a laminated copy of the Bill of Rights that Mr. Gill awarded to the best explanation, and he had told everyone on the way here that his father kept one in his office.

A woman came out of the courtroom doors, whispering angrily into her phone. "They can't shut the paper down. We printed what happened. Somebody has to be able to print what happened." A man in a rumpled suit followed her, shaking his head. Alexis's ears went hot. She wrote "newspaper???" in her notebook and underlined it three times.

"That's our thing," Vladimir whispered. "Speech and the press. Don't give me that look, I read ahead." He flipped through his handout and pointed at the page. "The First Amendment. Freedom of religion, speech, the press, peaceful assembly, and petitioning the government." He read it in one breath, like a spell.

Alexis stared at the list. Five things, and the second and third ones were what the angry woman needed. But which part would she explain, and how would she say it in words that sounded like her own and not like the handout? She tried a sentence in her head: the government cannot stop you from believing what you believe, saying what you think, printing what you find out, gathering peacefully, or asking the government to change things. That felt right, but she needed to test it.

She turned to Marc-Antoine. "Say the five things in the First Amendment without looking." He got religion, speech, and assembly, then stalled. Alexis covered her mouth so he wouldn't see her grin. She tried her sentence on Vladimir, who frowned like a rodent chewing a problem, then nodded. "Yeah. But say 'petitioning' like you mean it, not like a spelling word."

Mr. Gill appeared at the end of the hall with his clipboard, and the whole class went quiet. "Alexis," he said. Her prepared page on the Fifth Amendment suddenly seemed small in her hands, like a plan someone impulsive would have made, half-finished and aimed at the wrong target. She stepped forward anyway, closed her notebook, and started.

"It protects five things," she said. "Religion, speech, the press, peaceful assembly, and petitioning the government. In my own words: you can believe, you can speak, you can print, you can gather without violence, and you can demand the government listen. And today I watched a woman fight for the third one." Mr. Gill wrote something on his clipboard, and Marc-Antoine whispered, "I was going to say that."

activity: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
knowledge_domain: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
fact: A red herring is a false clue placed on purpose to lead readers toward the wrong conclusion, so not every hint in a story is real foreshadowing.
story:
The bus ride home took twenty-two minutes, and Justin had learned to use every one of them. He spread the short story across his knees, pencil ready, because tomorrow Ms. Reddy would call on his group to explain the foreshadowing, and he refused to be the one who said "I dunno" again.

Bailey leaned over the seat from behind. "Page four. The storm clouds when Mr. Ames locks the cellar door. That's foreshadowing, obviously. The cellar's where the treasure is."

Tianna slid into the seat across the aisle, holding her own copy with the margins already crowded. "And the ravens on the fence in paragraph two. Ravens mean death, so Ames dies."

"That's symbolism," Justin said, mostly to himself.

Baigan rolled her eyes. "Same thing."

"It's not." He tapped his pencil against the window. "Foreshadowing hints at what happens later. Symbolism is when something stands for a bigger idea." He had written both definitions on his hand during last period, and the ink was starting to smear.

Bailey wanted the group to win Ms. Reddy's challenge, a homework pass for the group with the best explanation, and she was willing to recruit half the bus to find clues if she had to. She pointed at the story again. "It doesn't matter. We have nine clues. Nine. Tianna's brother already guessed the ending. Ames hides the deed to the farm in the cellar, the storm floods it out, and he dies protecting it. Done."

Justin flipped to the last page, which he'd read ahead during lunch, alone at the end of the table. He didn't say anything about it. Instead he counted the clues, drawing a small dot beside each one, and noticed something odd. Eight of the clues pointed toward the cellar. One pointed away from it, the muddy boot prints going out the gate on page six, never explained.

"What are you doing?" Tianna asked.

"Testing something." He laid the page flat so the two columns of dots looked almost symmetrical, four on each side of the fold, with the boot prints sitting alone. "If all these are real hints, they should fit together. They don't."

"So cross out the boot prints," Bailey said.

But when he reached the ending again in his head, the cellar was empty. The deed was in the boot. The story had handed them nine shiny clues on purpose, and eight of them were lies.

"I figured it out," he said slowly. "There's a word for it. Ms. Reddy mentioned it once. A red herring. It's a false clue placed on purpose to lead readers toward the wrong conclusion." He looked up. "So not every hint in a story is real foreshadowing. We were supposed to fall for it."

Bailey stared at her nine clues. "So all my ravens..."

Tianna was already rewriting her notes. "The boot prints," she said, and grinned. "I'm putting them on poster board."

The bus lurched around the corner, and Justin slid his pencil under the clue that mattered most, the one everyone else had stepped over.

activity: going to a first school dance
knowledge_domain: going to a first school dance
fact: Line dances, in which a group repeats the same set of steps facing the same direction, let people dance together without needing a partner.
story:
Violet stared at the family group chat on her phone while her cousin Anouk typed, then deleted, then typed again. Finally the message landed: "Nobody's asked me to dance and I'm just standing by the punch table like a coat rack." Violet was in the gym with her class, waiting for the first school dance to start, and Anouk was at her own dance two towns over, texting the whole family for rescue.

Last year flashed into her mind: the fall talent show, when Anouk had stood in the wings with her violin, shaking so hard Violet had to walk out with her and pretend they were doing a duet of clapping. It hadn't fixed anything, really, but Anouk had laughed, and Violet had decided that was the job of cousins. Now the job was happening again, through a phone.

In the gym, the lights swept purple and blue, and Mr. Adebayo, who ran the dance committee, cranked up a song Violet actually knew. Something happened then that she hadn't expected. Instead of pairing off, half the eighth graders turned to face the same direction and started repeating the same handful of steps, over and over, like one giant machine made of people. Clara grabbed Violet's sleeve. "Come on, it's the electric slide." Violet followed her into the line, stomped right, stomped left, scuffed her heel twice, and after four repetitions her feet knew it without her telling them anything. She glanced around. Nobody in the line had a partner. Nobody needed one, because everyone was doing the same steps facing the same way, together.

Her thumbs moved fast. "Find the electric slide," she texted Anouk. "It's a line dance. Everyone faces the same direction and does the same steps, so you don't need a partner. Learn four steps and you're in." While she typed, Clara bumped her shoulder and pointed. A boy from Violet's math class, the one who never talked, hovered at the edge of the gym with his arms crossed like he was trying to insulate himself from the whole room. Clara was already waving him over before Violet could say anything. He shook his head, then shrugged, then shuffled into the line behind them, and by the second chorus he was keeping up, a little behind the beat but getting it.

The phone buzzed. A video: Anouk, in her gym, in a lopsided line of kids, doing a vigorous stomp-and-clap while someone's little brother filmed sideways and laughed. Then a second message: "A boy next to me said I'm doing it better than him. Nobody has a partner here either. It's actually kind of a privilege to be in this line, everybody's included by default."

The song ended and another started, faster. Violet slid the phone into her pocket, took the boy from math class by the elbow, and pointed him at the front row. "Watch their feet," she said. "Four steps. Count with me."

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: In Hungarian, a person's family name is written before the given name, the same order used in Chinese, Japanese and Korean names.
story:
The discussion circle had been going for ten minutes, and Katherine still hadn't said a word. Ms. Wardak had asked each of them to bring in something from home that showed where their family came from, and Katherine had brought her grandmother's old prescription slip, folded twice, because her grandmother had become a pharmacist the year she arrived in Canada and that slip was the first one she ever signed. But she was waiting, because Hamza looked like a storm cloud and nobody had noticed.

"That's my item," Hamza said finally, holding up a birthday card. "Except it's wrong, so it doesn't count." He passed it around, and Katherine saw the signature inside: Nagy László. "My grandfather signed it backwards. He's been having trouble with his hands, and now his brain too, maybe. He never makes mistakes. I don't want to put it up on the heritage board if it's a mistake."

Cian leaned over to look. "Maybe just don't use the card," he said, which was the kind of answer that solved nothing.

Katherine turned the card over in her hands. Something about the signature was germinating in her mind, a small idea she couldn't quite see yet. Her seatmate Wei's family name came first on every document she'd ever seen him write: Wei before the given name. Hamza's grandfather had done exactly the same thing, family name first, given name second. What if it wasn't a mistake at all?

"Ms. Wardak," she said, raising her hand, "can we test something? Wei, write your name on the board the way your family writes it. And Hamza's grandfather wrote Nagy László. Family name, then given name."

Wei wrote it. The class compared the two, and the pattern was unanimous across every example they could think of. "In Hungarian, a person's family name is written before the given name," Cian read slowly from his phone, "the same order used in Chinese, Japanese and Korean names."

"Your grandfather didn't make a mistake," Katherine told Hamza. "He wrote it the way Hungarian is written. Same as Wei's family does."

Hamza stared at the card for a long moment. Then he stood up and pinned it to the heritage board himself, right in the middle, before the class could vote on where it should go. "He's going to visit next month," he said. "I want him to see it there."

"Then he will," said Ms. Wardak, and moved on to the next item.

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In Japan, slurping noodles such as ramen and soba is considered acceptable at the table rather than rude.
story:
Brielle stood in the doorway of the Tanaka family's apartment holding a box of oranges so tightly that the cardboard dented. Margaux had invited her to a reunion dinner, and Brielle wanted more than anything to make a good impression, because Margaux's grandmother was visiting from Osaka and Brielle had never met her.

"You bow," Margaux whispered, demonstrating. "Not too deep, she's not the emperor." Brielle bowed, and the grandmother bowed back, and for one second they were stuck in a loop, each waiting for the other to stop, until Margaux's little brother laughed so hard he knocked over a shoe.

At the table, Dyson, who had come because he "loved free food," was telling everyone about his science project. "I measured the voltage of a potato battery," he said. "Two whole volts. My teacher looked at me like I'd invented fire." The grandmother smiled even though Dyson talked with his hands and nearly swept the soy sauce off the table.

Then the ramen arrived. Brielle lifted her bowl and took a careful, silent bite, the way she'd been taught at home, lips closed, fork tucked neatly. Around her, everyone was slurping. Margaux slurped. The grandmother slurped loudest of all, a long satisfied noise like a drain finishing its work. Dyson froze mid-slurp, spoon halfway to his mouth, and whispered, "Are we in trouble?"

Brielle watched and reasoned. Nobody's face looked angry. The grandmother slurped again and nodded approvingly at the noodles, then at Dyson. If slurping were rude, she wouldn't do it herself in front of guests. Brielle tested her idea quietly at first, then with more voltage in her efforts, a small brave slurp, then a bigger one. The grandmother looked up, beamed, and slurped back, which felt like being handed a trophy.

"It's actually good manners here," Margaux said, spraying a little broth. "Slurping means the noodles are good." Dyson immediately slurped so hard that a noodle escaped and slapped him on the chin. "Casualty," he announced. "I regret nothing."

After dinner, the grandmother pressed a small wrapped package into Brielle's hands, refusing to hear a single word about it being too much. Brielle bowed once more, this time exactly right, and the grandmother patted her arm. "You slurp like Osaka girl," she said, and pointed at the oranges Brielle had brought, which sat on the counter in a row like a small orange choir.

On the way out, Dyson asked if he could come back next week, and Margaux said, "Only if you bring oranges."

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: A checkable claim can be false; 'The Eiffel Tower is in Berlin' is a wrong factual claim, not an opinion.
story:
The poster had gone up overnight outside the library: "The Eiffel Tower is in Berlin, and honestly, it's the best tower in the world." Mason read it twice while the hallway smelled of floor wax and someone's vanilla lip balm. Ansh leaned over his shoulder and laughed. "That's so wrong it's almost funny."

"It's not wrong, it's my opinion," said Antonin, who had written it for the school's "Big Statements" board, where Ms. He let anyone post anything for a week. He crossed his arms, and the elastic band on his wrist snapped against his skin. "Opinions can't be wrong. That's the whole point."

Mason chewed on that through math class, tapping his pencil. Something about it itched. He wrote a note and folded it into a paper airplane, then thought better of throwing it and passed it to Ansh instead. "Question," the note read. "If I said the gym emits heat in winter because of the radiators, could that be an opinion? Or could we go check the radiators? Meet me at the library at lunch. Bring the atlas from geography." Ansh wrote back one word: "Atlas!" with a doodle of a detective hat.

At lunch, the library was cool and smelled like old paper. Ansh dropped the heavy atlas on the table with a thud that made a sixth grader look up and glare. Mason flipped to the map of Europe and spun the book toward Antonin. "Look. Berlin is here. Paris is way over here. The Eiffel Tower has a spot on the map, and it's next to Paris. So that part isn't an opinion. It's a claim, and we just checked it. A checkable claim can be false. 'The Eiffel Tower is in Berlin' is a wrong factual claim, not an opinion."

Antonin stared at the map for a long moment, running his thumb along the border between France and Germany. "Okay," he said slowly. "The location part, I give up, you got me. But the best-tower-in-the-world part?"

"That one's yours forever," Ansh said. "Nobody can check that with an atlas." Antonin grinned and pulled a marker from his backpack. They walked back to the board together, and Antonin crossed out "is in Berlin" and wrote above it in careful letters, "CORRECTION: located in Paris. Still the best tower in the world, and I will die on this hill."

Ms. He came around the corner with her coffee, read the correction, and raised her mug to Antonin. "Now that," she said, "is what I call a worthy antagonist to sloppy thinking."

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: In traditional Chinese culture white is worn for mourning at funerals, while in many Western weddings the bride wears white.
story:
Felix's kitchen smelled like dumplings and scallion pancakes, and every counter was covered with food. His older sister's engagement party started at two, and Declan had come over early to help because Felix had promised him first crack at the karaoke machine afterward. They were stapling white paper flowers to a banner when Felix's grandmother came through the front door, took one look at the living room, and stopped so suddenly that her tote bag swung forward and hit her hip.

She said something quick in Cantonese, and Felix's mom hurried over. The two of them went back and forth in low voices while Declan stood on a chair holding a stapler, pretending to be very busy with a flower. Felix's face went pink. "She thinks the whole room looks like a funeral," he muttered.

Declan climbed down slowly. A funeral? The room had white streamers, white flowers, a white tablecloth, all because Felix's sister had said her fiancé's family "wanted the classic look." Declan had been to his aunt's wedding last summer, and the bride had worn a big white gown, and everyone had cried because they were happy. Same color, he thought, two completely different days. It was like the time his bus route changed and he'd blamed the driver, when really the detour downtown was the hidden cause. You couldn't see the reason. You had to test it.

"Can we borrow the red stuff from the basement?" Declan asked Felix. "The lanterns from Chinese New Year?" Felix's mom was already halfway down the stairs, which Declan took as a good sign. He started pulling down the white banner, and Felix stuffed the paper flowers into a garbage bag. "My sister's going to freak," Felix said, but he was grinning as he said it.

When Felix's sister arrived with her fiancé, she stopped in the doorway exactly the way her grandmother had. "Where's my white theme?" she demanded. The fiancé, though, was staring at the red lanterns with what looked like relief. His parents, it turned out, had been commuting two hours each way and worrying the whole ride about the decorations, though nobody would say why until the grandmother finally did. Felix translated, keeping it short. "White is what we wear for mourning," he said. "At funerals. Not here." His sister looked at her fiancé, and then at the red lanterns glowing above the food, and something seemed to click into place between the two families, like two parallel lines finally crossing.

"I can wear my red dress to the wedding," the fiancé's mother said, patting her handbag as if checking for it. "You can wear your white one," she told Felix's sister. "Different meanings, both beautiful." The grandmother nodded once, briskly, and pointed at Declan. He had no idea what she said, but Felix laughed. "She wants to know if the kid with the stapler eats dumplings."

Declan held up the stapler like a trophy. "Point me to the dumplings," he said.

activity: to ask for directions in a new language and understand the answer
knowledge_domain: to ask for directions in a new language and understand the answer
fact: Language learners can usually understand more words than they can say, so a learner may follow spoken directions they could not yet give themselves.
story:
The rain was coming, everyone in Mouhamed's kitchen agreed, and the radio man said it in Wolof, a language Hannah had been hearing for exactly three days. She caught the word for precipitation and nothing else. Mouhamed translated anyway: storms by evening. That mattered, because Mouhamed's mother needed onions from the little shop two streets over before it started pouring, and both he and his mother had to watch the stove.

"I'll go," Hannah said. Then, quieter, "If you teach me how to ask."

Mouhamed grinned. "You need one sentence. Ana waruka?" He said it slowly, twice, and Hannah repeated it until he stopped wincing. He told her the shop's name was the equivalent of "the place of onions," which made her laugh, and that his grandmother would be sitting outside it, because she always was. What he did not teach her was a single word for left, right, straight, or stop, because his mother was calling him back to the stove. "You'll be fine," he said, and pushed her out the door.

The shop was not where she expected. Hannah asked her one sentence at a first woman, who waved her up the street, and then at a boy on a bicycle, who pointed at a corner and let loose a river of Wolof that went on for what felt like a full minute. Her stomach dropped. Then, inside the rush of sound, words started surfacing, one by one, like stones in shallow water. She knew that one, from listening at Mouhamed's table. And that one. Turn. At the thing with the blue door, the boy had said, and then the word for "two," and then a word she was almost sure meant "market." She nodded as if she'd understood every bit of it, thanked him, and walked.

Blue door. Then a second one. Then the smell of spice and the sound of the market, loud even under the first fat drops of rain. And there, under an awning, sat an old woman who looked up and said something long and warm.

Hannah froze. In Wolof she could ask where something was, and she could say thank you, and that was all. She could not have repeated one word of the boy's directions if her life depended on it. Yet her feet had carried her here anyway. She handed over Mouhamed's mother's money, took the onions, and ducked into the rain.

Back at the house, dripping on the mat, she held up the bag. "I didn't understand all of it," she said. "But I understood enough."

Mouhamed's mother lifted the onions like a trophy. "Enough," she emphasized, "is everything."

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
fact: Regression to the mean means unusually bad days tend to be followed by more ordinary ones, so people who try a remedy when symptoms are worst may improve even if it does nothing.
story:
Samantha pressed her library book flat on the table and glared at it, as if it were the book's fault that her science project was due Friday. Her grandmother had drunk a cup of willow tea last month for a terrible headache and sworn the tea had cured her. Now Samantha had to figure out whether that was a scientific claim or just a story, and she had exactly one week to do it.

"You look like you're fighting the book," said John, sliding into the chair across from her with his own stack of research. He wanted his project to be about volcanoes, and he had already filled six note cards, which Samantha found quietly annoying.

"My grandma says her tea fixed her headache," Samantha said. "I thought that would be easy to prove. It's not."

Ms. Oliveira, the librarian, paused at their table with a cart of returns. "Tea and headaches," she said. "That's an interesting one. Let me know if you need the medical shelf." She rolled on toward the biography section, humming something eccentric and cheerful that Samantha could not identify.

Samantha remembered the night of the headache. She had been doing homework at the kitchen table when her grandmother came in holding her head, saying the pain was the worst she'd had in years. Grandmother had sipped the tea slowly, gone to bed early, and woken up fine. "That tea," she had announced at breakfast, "is a miracle." Samantha had believed her completely, right up until Ms. Oliveira had asked the class on Monday to separate tested evidence from single stories.

She pulled a piece of paper toward her and wrote: grandma had the worst headache in years. Then she wrote: the next day, she was better. Then, slowly, she added a third line: wouldn't a very bad day be followed by an ordinary one anyway? She flipped through the book she'd found, and there it was, a short paragraph saying that unusually bad days tend to be followed by more ordinary ones, so people who try a remedy when symptoms are worst may improve even if it does nothing. "So even if the tea did nothing," she whispered, "Grandma would probably have eased off anyway."

"What are you muttering about?" John asked.

"Regression to the mean," Samantha said, tapping the page. "It's a thing. It's why my grandma's story doesn't prove the tea worked."

John leaned over and read the paragraph twice. "So for your project, you'd need to test a whole bunch of headaches, not just one."

"And I can't do that," Samantha said, deflating. Then she sat up. "But I can critique the claim. I can show exactly why one person's story can't prove a cure." She began writing so fast her pen squeaked.

Julia arrived with her backpack still on one shoulder and peered at the paper. "You're smiling," she said. "That's suspicious."

"My project isn't ruined. It's better than the volcano thing."

"It is not," said John, but he was grinning.

At home that evening, Samantha called her grandmother and told her the whole plan, then asked if she would help by writing down her headaches and how bad they were, every day, tea or no tea. "You want to expose my tea as a fake," her grandmother said.

"I want to find out what's true," Samantha said. "The tea might be fine. One story just can't show it."

Her grandmother was quiet for a moment. "All right," she said. "I'll keep the chart. And I'll keep drinking the tea, because I like it."

On Friday, Samantha stood in front of the class with her chart and her grandmother's terrible-headache night drawn as one tall spike on a graph. "Here's the day she drank the tea," she said, tapping the spike. "And here's the next day. The question is, what made the difference?" She looked at John in the second row, and he gave her a thumbs-up, and she flipped to her next slide.

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
knowledge_domain: recovering from a cold or flu at home
fact: According to the U.S. CDC, people with the flu are most contagious during the first three days of their illness.
story:
Violet sat in the waiting room of the doctor's office with a tissue in one hand and her mother's phone in the other, scrolling the list of people who had said they were going to Mina's birthday party. Forty-three names. Lance had written "wouldn't miss it" under his. Violet was on day two of the flu, and her fever had finally dropped, which meant she felt almost normal, which meant the party was still possible.

The nurse called her back, took her temperature, and said it was coming down. While her mother filled out a form at the front desk, Violet waited by the examination room door and noticed a laminated poster on the wall. It said the flu spreads most easily from person to person, and that according to the U.S. CDC, people with the flu are most contagious during the first three days of their illness. She read it twice. Day one had been Sunday, the worst day, the day she had slept through everything. Today was Monday. That was day two.

In the car, she counted on her fingers. "If I go to the party Saturday, that's day six," she said. "I'd be way past three days."

"Count again," her mother said, pulling out of the parking lot. "You got sick Saturday."

Violet's fingers stopped. Sunday had been day one only if the flu had started Sunday, but she remembered shivering at dinner on Saturday and going to bed early, before Mina's messages started. Saturday was day one. Sunday was day two. Monday, today, was day three. She stared out the window at the pharmacy and the bus stop and did the math one more time, slower. Today was still inside the window. If she went to school tomorrow and hugged Mina and grabbed the same pizza slice tray as Lance, she would be right at the edge of it, and the poster had not said day four was safe, only that the first three were the worst.

At home she texted Mina: I can't come Friday. I'm on day three of the flu and people are most contagious the first three days, so I don't want to get everyone. Mina sent back a picture of the guest list with Violet's name moved to the top, under a heading that said "save this slice."

Violet spent the afternoon testing her own theory. She wiped down the TV remote, then the doorknobs, because if she was still contagious, the virus could be on things she touched, even though she could not see anything there. She found the disinfectant spray under the sink and read the label, which had a warning in small print that said corrosive, so she pulled on the rubber gloves her mother kept with the mop. By dinner she had cleaned every surface she could remember touching since Saturday. It was not the same as being at the party, but it was something she could do, a small economy of favors: she stayed home, and Mina saved her a slice, and Lance promised to video the cake.

On Saturday morning, day six, Violet's throat was fine and her temperature was normal. She walked to Mina's house carrying the gift she had wrapped herself, a sketchbook and a set of markers, and when Mina opened the door she held out the present and said, "I'm past day three, so I'm allowed to hug you now."

activity: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
knowledge_domain: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
fact: Airplane mode turns off a phone's radio signals, including the cellular connection it uses for calls and texts.
story:
The phone store smelled like cardboard and new plastic, and Ruby held the display model so carefully that her hands ached. Her father had said one phone, one case, and a decision in twenty minutes, because her little brother's soccer practice started at five. Mr. Martínez, the neighbour who had driven them, leaned on the counter and watched Ruby compare two phones like a judge weighing evidence. "Take your time," he said, though everyone knew she had none. At last she chose the smaller one, sky blue, and a case with a dinosaur on it that her father pretended not to like.

By the time they got home there were only forty minutes before Ruby had promised to meet Alexis at her house to finish their science project, a poster about local birds. Ruby charged the phone just long enough for the screen to wake, then ran three blocks with the phone bouncing in her pocket. She had earned it, too. Last spring she had volunteered to donate her whole weekend to the animal shelter's cleanup day, and afterward her father had called her "eloquent on the subject of deserving a phone," which was his way of teasing her for arguing so well.

At Alexis's house the poster went fine until Alexis's mother announced dinner in twenty minutes, which meant the project had to be done by then. That was when Alexis frowned at her own phone and said, "Thierry was going to text me the citation for that bird website. He promised. Nothing's come through." They waited. Alexis tapped the screen, held the phone up toward the window like she could catch a signal in her hand, and even turned the phone off and on again. Still nothing, and the clock on the wall crept toward dinner.

Ruby thought about her own new phone, still in her pocket, and about how Alexis's phone had been silent since they started gluing feathers onto the poster. She remembered something she'd noticed in the store, a tiny airplane icon in the corner of the display model's screen. She had tapped it once out of curiosity and seen the signal bars disappear, then tapped it again and watched them return. Now she leaned over Alexis's shoulder and looked at the top of the screen. There it was: the same little airplane. "Airplane mode," Ruby said, pointing.

Alexis stared at the icon. "My little brother had my phone in the car," she said slowly. "He must have turned it on." She tapped it off, and before she even set the phone down it buzzed twice, fast, like a held breath finally let out. Thierry's messages scrolled in, one right after another, along with the link they needed. Alexis read the citation out loud while Ruby wrote it at the bottom of the poster in her neatest letters, and the last feather was glued down just as Alexis's mother called from the kitchen. Ruby felt her own phone buzz once in her pocket, and she grinned at Alexis without checking it yet. "Ten more minutes," Alexis's mother said from the doorway, holding up the timer.

activity: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak
knowledge_domain: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak
fact: Robert's Rules of Order, a guide to running meetings fairly, was first published in 1876 by U.S. Army officer Henry Martyn Robert.
story:
Florence pushed her peas around her plate while her dad told her grandfather about the new tenant in the upstairs apartment, a quiet man who fixed bicycles in the garage. She was only half listening. Her mind was back in the school library, at the Nature Club meeting she had run that afternoon, where Blakely and Zoe had ended up shouting over each other about the fund-raiser until the bell rang and nothing got decided. Next week she had to run it again, and the thought made her stomach tight.

"Something wrong with the peas?" her grandfather asked. He always noticed.

"The club meeting," Florence said. "I'm president, but I can't get anyone to stop talking at once. Zoe thinks we should sell seed packets. Blakely wants a bake sale. Mr. Watanabe says if we can't decide by Friday, the school will give our table at the spring fair to the chess club." She set down her fork. "It's like everyone gets louder and nobody gets heard."

Her grandfather chewed slowly, then pushed back his chair. "Come with me a minute." He led her to the bookshelf in the hallway, the one with the dusty top rows nobody touched, and pulled down a small brown book so old its spine was soft. "This was your great-grandmother's. I nearly gave it away last spring. See what you think."

Florence opened it on the hall table. The pages smelled like cedar. It was a guide to running meetings, all about agendas and motions and taking turns so every person got to speak once before anyone spoke twice. "Robert's Rules of Order," she read on the title page. "It says here it was first published in 1876. By a U.S. Army officer named Henry Martyn Robert." She looked up. "An army officer wrote a book about being fair at meetings?"

"Goes back further than your club does," her grandfather said. "Take it home."

That week, Florence wrote an agenda on a sheet of loose-leaf: old business, then the seed packets, then the bake sale, then a vote. She made a rule, borrowed straight from the book, that anyone wanting to speak raised a hand and got called on, and that discussion of one item had to cease before the next one began. When Zoe started to interrupt, Florence said, "Hold that thought, it's next on the agenda," and Zoe actually sat back and waited. Blakely got her whole argument out without a single shout. Then Zoe did. The vote was close, six to five, seed packets, and Blakely shrugged and said, "At least I got to talk."

On Friday, Florence carried the old book to Mr. Watanabe's classroom and set it on his desk so he could see they had a plan now. He read the title page, then raised his eyebrows at her. "This is a loaner," Florence told him. "Temporary. Grandpa says it stays in the family."

activity: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
knowledge_domain: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
fact: Running the second half of a race faster than the first is called a negative split; running the first half faster is called a positive split.
story:
Caleb stood at the starting line in the school gym, where cones marked four laps of a short oval because the track outside was still buried in snow. He had lost the eight-hundred-metre race at the last meet by blowing up halfway through, and today he intended to figure out why. The problem was invisible. He couldn't see his energy draining away, but he could see the results: a fast first lap, then legs like wet sand on the second.

Davin jogged up beside him. "I've been thinking about our race," Davin said. "Your first lap was way faster than mine, but I caught you at the end. My second lap was quicker than my first. Running the second half faster than the first is called a negative split. Running the first half faster is called a positive split." He pulled a crumpled paper from his pocket with both their lap times on it, which they had copied off the results sheet outside the caretaker's residence next to the gym.

Caleb studied the numbers. His first lap had been three seconds quicker than his second. Davin's second lap had been four seconds quicker than his first. So Davin had run a negative split, and Caleb had run a positive split, and Davin had won. Caleb couldn't see the pattern working inside his own legs, but he could see it on paper, and it repeated exactly. "I want to test something," he said. "Next time trial, I run the first lap slow on purpose. Deliberately slow. If I die on the second lap anyway, the idea is wrong."

Pascal, who was holding the stopwatch, laughed. "That's backwards. Everyone knows you go out hard and hang on." Caleb said that maybe everyone was biased, because going out hard felt brave and slowing down felt like quitting, even if it won races. Pascal shrugged and agreed to time it anyway.

Ms. Kowalski blew her whistle from the stage at the end of the gym, and the three of them set off. Caleb counted his steps and held himself back while Pascal and Davin surged ahead. It felt awful. At halfway he was trailing by half the gym, but his breathing was even and his legs still answered when he asked them to go. He began to pick runners off. He passed Davin on the third lap, and on the last stretch he caught Pascal two cones from the finish and leaned across the line first.

Afterward, all three of them sat on the bleachers with the stopwatch, and Caleb made them read out his laps. First lap slower, second lap faster. A negative split, on purpose, and it had worked once. It might not work every time, and he would have to evaluate it again at the next time trial before he trusted it. Davin clapped him on the shoulder. "Same race next week," Davin said. "This time I'm racing your way."

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
knowledge_domain: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
fact: A pill organizer has a compartment for each day of the week, so an empty compartment shows that day's dose has already been taken.
story:
The arrivals board at the airport flipped from DELAYED to LANDED, and Luke stood on his toes even though it changed nothing about his view. His grandmother was coming to stay for a whole week, and he had promised his mom he would hold the sign he'd made, mostly so she could find them in the crowd. GRANDMA FRIDA, it said, in letters so large that a man beside him asked whether she was famous. "Only to me," Luke said, which made the man laugh. Then the doors opened, and there she was, dragging a suitcase with one wheel that spun in the approximate direction she never intended to go.

At home, things went well for two days. Then, on Tuesday morning, Luke found her standing at the kitchen counter, frowning at a plastic box with seven little lids in a row. "Did I take my morning pills?" she asked. "I can't remember, and I don't want to take them twice." Luke picked up the box and turned it over in his hands, curious how anyone was supposed to solve a problem like that. It was like trying to figure out whether the fridge light goes off when the door closes. You couldn't see the answer directly. You had to look for evidence.

He opened the lid marked MON and found it empty, and the lid marked TUE was empty too. The WED compartment still held its little cluster of pills, and so did THU through SUN. "Wait," he said slowly. "If you'd forgotten Monday, that compartment would be full. Two empty compartments means two doses already taken. It's Tuesday, so today's is the empty one." His grandmother peered at the box. "You mean the box remembers for me?" "The box testifies," Luke said grandly. "If my teacher asks me to cite my sources, I will cite a plastic container." She laughed so hard she had to sit down.

At school that afternoon, Luke told Yanis and Mathew about it during lunch. Mathew said it was like a metaphor for memory, a machine doing the remembering for you. "Not a metaphor," Luke said. "An actual box. Metaphors don't have lids." Yanis pointed out that the whole thing only worked if she loaded it correctly at the start of the week, which was the part Luke found the most interesting. A system was only as good as its weakest Sunday night.

The next morning Luke came downstairs and found his grandmother opening WED, shaking the pills into her palm. "Tuesday's compartment was empty," she announced, "so I knew it was Wednesday." She looked rather pleased with herself. Luke grinned and got the orange juice. "So," he said, sliding the glass across the counter, "same time tomorrow?"

activity: to call plays as a point guard and run a pick and roll
knowledge_domain: to call plays as a point guard and run a pick and roll
fact: The NBA adopted a 24-second shot clock for its 1954-55 season, requiring a team to attempt a shot within 24 seconds of getting the ball.
story:
The court behind the rec center had one good rim and one bent one, an impoverished patch of asphalt with cracks running through the key. Addison was running point for the first time in a real game, and her team was losing 8 to 6. The other team's best player, Zachariah, kept calling for the ball and then holding it, dribbling in place, letting the clock on his phone tick away whole minutes while nobody scored.

"That's not even basketball," Elaine said, wiping sweat off her forehead. "He's just standing there."

Addison had been watching anyway, not the ball but the other team. Every time she called for a screen, their big man switched onto the roller and their guard stayed with the ball. But when Elaine set a screen without Addison signaling, nobody switched, and Elaine slipped free under the rim twice. The pattern was invisible unless you compared the two situations, and Addison thought she had it: the defense was reading her voice, not the movement itself.

"Give me the ball," she said. She took it to the top, and this time she called nothing. Elaine set the screen silently, and the defenders both stayed on the ball, exactly as Addison predicted. Elaine rolled, Addison fired the pass between two arms, and Elaine laid it in. 8 to 7. Zachariah called timeout out of pure frustration.

"We should get a shot clock," Elaine shouted across the half court. "Like the NBA."

"We don't have a clock," Zachariah said.

"Use your phone. The NBA adopted a 24-second shot clock for its 1954-55 season," Elaine said. "You have to attempt a shot within 24 seconds of getting the ball. So you can't just stand there."

"You made that up," Zachariah said. "Basketball didn't always have clocks." But he couldn't contradict her with anything specific, and his own teammates were tired of standing around, so one of them held up a phone and started the timer. Zachariah got the ball and, for the first time all afternoon, had to attack.

Addison kept her discovery quiet for two possessions. Then, with 14 seconds on the clock and her team down 8 to 9, she brought the ball up and called the play out loud anyway. "Elaine, high screen!" The big man switched just like she expected, and instead of using the screen, Addison split off the opposite way into the space he had abandoned. She pulled up at the free throw line. The ball hit the back rim, bounced straight up, and dropped through.

Elaine grabbed her by both shoulders. "You called it out loud on purpose?"

"Nine to nine," Addison said, backing toward the top of the key. "Watch the phone. Twenty-four seconds."

activity: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak
knowledge_domain: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak
fact: Under Robert's Rules, a majority vote means more than half of the votes cast.
story:
Claire carried her clipboard down to the lake dock like it was made of gold, because taped to it was the first official agenda of the Camp Birchwood Trading Post Club. Item one: opening remarks. Item two: what to do with the club's fifteen dollars. Item three: vote. She had been meticulous about it, rewriting the whole thing twice because the first version had put the vote before the discussion, which Dahlia said was like chewing before the sandwich arrived.

"Order!" Claire called, standing on a flat rock that served as the podium. Nine campers sat on the dock, plus Adele, who was lying on the dock with her hat over her face.
