"We'll go down the agenda one item at a time, and everyone who wants to talk gets a turn before we move on. Raise hands, and I'll keep a list."

It worked better than she'd hoped, mostly. Item two produced a flood of ideas: a telescope, a repair kit for the canoes, a giant watermelon for the end-of-camp party. Then Marco, who could not sustain interest in any topic for more than two minutes, moved that they buy the watermelon, and Mr. Adeyemi, the nature counselor who had wandered over to watch, seconded it just to keep things moving.

"All in favor of the watermelon?" Claire counted five hands. "Opposed?" Four hands, including Adele's, whose hat slid off as she shot her arm up. Marco immediately demanded a recount, then changed his mind halfway through and said, "Wait, no, the recount will make us miss swimming."

"Then it passed, right? Five beats four," said Dahlia.

"Hold on," Claire said. Two people hadn't voted at all. She counted the dock again, tapping each head with her pencil. Eleven members, five yes, four no, two nothing. She remembered the rule from the dusty club handbook she'd found in the craft cabin, the one nobody else would touch because a spider lived in it. "A majority vote means more than half of the votes cast. Not more than half the club. Just the votes actually cast."

"So five out of nine," Adele said, sitting up, suddenly interested. "Nine votes cast, and five is more than half of nine."

"It passed!" Marco pumped both fists and nearly rolled off the dock.

"But what if the two who didn't vote show up tomorrow and hate watermelons?" asked one of the non-voters, looking worried.

"Then they should have voted," Adele said. "That's the whole trick of it. You have to show up."

Claire wrote MOTION PASSED, 5-4 on her agenda, feeling like a real chairperson, whatever that was. "Next meeting, Thursday, same rock. Item one will be assigning someone to carry the watermelon."

Marco raised his hand. "Point of order. Can the watermelon be my co-chair?"

"It can be whatever you want," Claire said, "as long as it doesn't try to run the meeting."

activity: going to a first school dance
knowledge_domain: going to a first school dance
fact: Nervousness triggers the release of adrenaline, which speeds up the heart and pulls blood away from the stomach, causing the "butterflies" feeling.
story:
Jules's bedroom smelled like hair spray and mint gum, and Hailey sat on the bed holding a diagonal-striped dress she wasn't sure about. The dance started in forty minutes. Her stomach had been doing a strange floating thing since lunch, and she wanted to know why.

"Your hands are freezing," Jules said, grabbing one. "Mine too. And my stomach feels like it's full of moths."

"That's the exact feeling," Hailey said. She had been thinking about it all afternoon. "Hayden said his stomach flips and his heart pounds before he even gets somewhere scary. At his last game, before the whistle, his heart was going so fast he could hear it." She frowned. "Why would a stomach and a heart both act weird at the same time? They don't even do the same job."

"Maybe you're just hungry," Jules said, chewing her gum.

Hailey tested that idea by eating half a granola bar. The floating feeling stayed exactly where it was, so hunger wasn't the cause. Something else had to be making it happen. She counted her own pulse with two fingers on her wrist, watching the clock, and got ninety-four beats in a minute. Sitting still on a bed, that was fast. Her heart was racing like she'd been running laps, only she hadn't moved.

The doorbell rang, and Hayden came in still wearing his soccer warmup, holding an ice pack to his head. "Missed a ball at practice," he said. "The coach thinks it might be a concussion, so my mom has to watch me tonight. She's driving us to the dance and staying in the parking lot the whole time."

"You're still coming?" Jules said.

"Skipping the first dance of middle school? No." He sat down heavily in the desk chair. "Also my stomach is doing the flip thing again, and my heart is thumping like crazy. I haven't even walked in yet. Am I sick?"

Hailey leaned forward. She lined up what she knew like clues. Fear of the dance, then racing heart, then the floaty stomach, always together, always before something scary, never during something calm. "I think it's one thing causing all of it," she said slowly. "When you're nervous, your body lets out something called adrenaline. It speeds up your heart. And it pulls blood away from your stomach. That's the flip. People call them butterflies."

"Wait, so the butterflies are real?" Hayden said.

"They're a real feeling with a real cause. Nothing's actually wrong with you." Hailey checked her pulse again, thinking. "So if being nervous makes it, then being less nervous should stop it. What makes you not nervous?"

Jules and Hayden looked at each other. "Music," they said at the same time.

Jules turned on her speaker, loud, and Hayden drummed the ice pack against his knee in time to the beat. They jumped around for one whole song, the diagonal dress forgotten on the bed, and when the song ended Hailey took Hayden's wrist and counted. Eighty-two.

"It's going down," she said, grinning. "It actually works."

"Then we petition the DJ for this exact song," Hayden said, "the second we get in."

In the car, all three of them were quiet until the gym doors came into view, glowing. Hailey's stomach floated once more, high and light, and this time she just smiled at it.

"Ready?" Jules asked.

Hailey opened the car door. "Butterflies and all."

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: In a fair test, everything except the variable being tested is kept the same, such as the amount, the temperature and the timing.
story:
Something was eating Logan's tomatoes, and it had excellent taste, because it only took the best ones. Each morning he found another perfect red fruit gnawed down to a green ring, always on the low branches, always overnight.

"Raccoons," said Kellan, leaning over the fence between their yards. "Big ones. Possibly a bear."

"It's not a bear," Logan said. "It's something smaller. And it comes at night." He couldn't see the culprit, so he decided to do what Ms. Bakker called working like a scientist: guess, then test. His guess, his hypothesis, was that the eater was a bird, because the bites were high on the fruit and messy, like pecking. Caius, who was over by the shed holding a garden fork like a knight, had a different hypothesis. "Mice," he said. "They climb."

"Then let's test it," Logan said. He had overheard Ms. Bakker next door telling someone about her students' plant experiment, and one phrase had stuck in his head: a fair test keeps everything except the one thing you're testing exactly the same, same amount, same temperature, same timing. He figured that rule could work here too.

They set up two tomato plants in pots, side by side in the middle of the garden, with the same amount of water, in the same temperature, checked at the same time each morning. On one plant they stretched netting over the top, tall enough that a bird couldn't reach through. The other stayed bare. If the birds were guilty, the netted plant would be safe and the bare one would get eaten. If the mice were guilty, both plants would get eaten, because mice would just climb the netting, and Caius would get to look smug.

The first morning brought an ominous discovery: the bare plant had two bites taken from it, and the netted plant was untouched. Logan felt a flicker of triumph but refused to diagnose the case as solved on one night of evidence. That felt like deciding a whole season from one at-bat, as his coach would say. They repeated the setup, same amounts, same spot, same timing, for three more nights. Same result each time.

"It was birds," Kellan said, in the tone of someone who had guessed wrong and was now guessing after the answer was known.

"That's what the test says," Logan said. He felt a small obligation to be fair about it, since Caius had been wrong and was taking it with more dignity than expected. Caius was still holding the fork.

Ms. Bakker looked over the fence on her way to her car, nodded at the two pots, and said, "One variable, everything else the same?" Logan held up two fingers. "Four nights." She gave him a thumbs-up and drove off, which felt like the highest grade he'd received all year.

That evening he netted the whole row, every plant, and stood back to admire it. Somewhere overhead, a fat robin watched him from the power line, un-netted, patient.

"We'll see about tomorrow," Logan told it.

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: In a 1977 study, Lynn Hasher and colleagues found that people rated statements as more likely to be true after seeing them repeated, whether or not they were true.
story:
The rumor said the vending machine in the east hallway had taken Maisy's dollar and given her nothing back, and it had spread so fast that by Wednesday half the seventh grade was refusing to buy anything, which was a problem for Bentley, because he had spent his entire allowance on a candy resale scheme that depended on that machine's reputation.

He sat in Ms. Moretti's history classroom trying to figure out where the rumor had come from. Nobody had actually seen Maisy lose the dollar. Maeve said she'd heard it from a kid in gym, who heard it from someone else. Bentley counted on his fingers under the desk. He had heard the story five separate times himself, and he'd caught himself telling it twice.

"You only believe it because you keep hearing it," he whispered to Maeve. "That's it. That's the whole reason."

"So?"

"So it's like when they play the same cereal commercial over and over and then you think the cereal must be good." He leaned closer. "People did a study in 1977. Lynn Hasher and some other researchers. They found that people rated statements as more likely to be true after seeing them repeated, whether or not they were true."

Maeve looked skeptical. "Where did you learn that?"

"Ms. Moretti's propaganda unit. Yesterday. I was actually listening, for once."

Ms. Moretti rapped the board. "Moving on. Wartime posters. Notice this one says everyone is buying war bonds. That's a bandwagon appeal. It doesn't give you a reason; it just says everyone's doing it, so you should too." She pointed at a poster with a famous actor's face. "And here's a celebrity testimonial. And this headline calls the enemy 'savage.' Loaded words."

Bentley raised his hand. "Is repeating something a lot also one of those?"

"It can be, yes. Advertising works partly on it." She moved on to agriculture posters from the same era, full of waving wheat and words like "abundance."

At lunch, Bentley ran his test. He told Maisy, loudly, that the machine had been inspected by the district and was totally fine, then got Maeve to mention it to two kids at the next table, then asked a seventh grader to bring it up one more time by the water fountain. By the end of the day, three separate people had told Bentley the machine was fine as if they'd known it all along. One of them had been spreading the original rumor at breakfast.

"You repeated it," Maeve said, catching him by the doors. "You used the exact trick you were complaining about."

"I know," Bentley said. He fed his last dollar into the machine and pressed B4. The candy bar dropped, and the change clinked down, and a kid behind him in line said, "See? Everybody's using it again."

activity: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
knowledge_domain: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
fact: You may never divide both sides of an equation by zero, because division by zero has no answer.
story:
The community centre math club met on Thursdays in the room with the broken radiator, and Vincent had missed three weeks because of his paper route. Now he sat hunched over a worksheet, pencil ticking, trying to remember what Mr. Chukwu had taught about equations. He knew the rule well enough to say it: whatever you do to one side, you do to the other. Subtract three from both sides, and the sides stay balanced like a scale. Divide both sides by four, same thing. But the problems in front of him kept coming out wrong, and he could not see why.

"Try number seven," said Willem, sliding his chair over. Willem finished worksheets the way other kids finished crisps, in about ninety seconds. "Just get x alone."

"I know that part," Vincent said. "It's after that it falls apart."

Across the table, Irene was waving a page in the air. "Mr. Chukwu, I proved one equals two. Look." She read it out, step by step, starting from a equals b. Multiply both sides by a. Subtract b squared. Factor. Divide. And there it was, 1 equals 2, tidy as anything.

Mr. Chukwu raised an eyebrow and told her the proof was counterfeit, and that finding the hidden flaw in it would earn her a place at the regional team table. That was the table Vincent wanted. The team had four seats, and the tryouts were in two weeks, and Willem already had one.

That night Vincent copied Irene's proof onto graph paper and dismantled it line by line, testing each step the way you test a bridge, one plank at a time. Every line looked legal. Multiply both sides, fine. Subtract from both sides, fine. Factor, fine. Then he stopped at the division. Divide both sides by a minus b. He frowned at it. He plugged in numbers. If a equals b, then a minus b equals zero. He wrote it out, circled it, and sat very still.

The next Thursday he got there early and found Irene by the whiteboard. "Line five," he said. "You divide by a minus b. But if a equals b, that's zero. You may never divide both sides of an equation by zero, because division by zero has no answer."

Irene stared at the proof, then at him, then burst out laughing. "You sneak. I checked every line."

"You checked them forward," Vincent said. He picked up the marker and drew a fat circle around the sneaky step. The nib squeaked against the board.

Mr. Chukwu came in with the tryout list in one hand and read the whiteboard over their shoulders. He said nothing, but he wrote a second name at the top of the list, and slid it across the table. Vincent's name sat beside Willem's.

"First practice is Saturday," Mr. Chukwu said. "Bring the marker. And bring that circle."

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Muscle soreness after new or hard exercise usually peaks 24 to 72 hours later, not right away; this is called delayed onset muscle soreness.
story:
Emmett floated home from the first basketball practice of the season. His legs felt springy, his shot felt smooth, and he told his dad that tryouts had been nothing. "Easiest practice of my life," he said. On Wednesday, two days later, he woke up and nearly fell over trying to climb the stairs. His thighs burned like someone had filled them with sand. He hobbled into the kitchen gripping the railing.

At school he found Marylou and Cayden at the lunch table. "Walk it off," Cayden said, chewing his sandwich. But Emmett was frowning at the ceiling, thinking. Practice had been Monday. He'd felt fine Monday night, fine Tuesday morning, and now Wednesday he could barely sit down without lowering himself with both arms on the desk. Why hadn't it hurt right away? "That's weird," he said. "If the practice caused it, the soreness should've shown up right after. Unless it's like a delayed reaction." Cayden offered his testimony: the same thing had happened to him after his first week of swimming lessons, fine that day, wrecked two days later. "Three kids on my old team said that too," Marylou added, and Emmett wrote the pattern in his notebook: fine first day, worst on day two or day three.

That night he searched the internet and found the name for it. "Delayed onset muscle soreness," he read out loud to himself. Muscle soreness after new or hard exercise usually peaked twenty-four to seventy-two hours later, not right away. He sat back. So that was the rule. Then his stomach dropped, because the first game was Saturday, and if the pattern held, today and tomorrow would be the worst days, right up against tipoff.

He had an idea and decided to test it. Thursday, Mr. Qureshi supervised the open gym hour, so Emmett asked if he could use a side hoop. He didn't sprint or jump. He jogged gentle laps, took slow set shots, and stretched while Marylou timed him. His theory was simple: if the soreness was already peaking, moving lightly couldn't make a new peak, because he wasn't doing anything new or hard. By Friday afternoon the sand in his legs had drained away. He climbed the bleachers two steps at a time and grinned down at Cayden.

Saturday morning the team bus rolled up to the neutral gym across town, where neither side would have home fans, and Emmett bounced on his toes in the layup line. His legs felt light and quick. "Whatever you did," Cayden whispered, "do it before every game." Emmett spun the ball on his finger, caught it, and said, "Science, my friend. Science." Then the whistle blew, and he broke toward the basket.

activity: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
knowledge_domain: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
fact: A primary source is something made at the time by a person who lived through an event, such as a settler's diary, while a secondary source is written later by someone studying it.
story:
Cameron crouched beside the stone wall of the war memorial, holding his phone flat against a faded plaque. His history project was due Monday, and it had to explain why people moved west in the 1800s, using a primary source. The problem was he had picked the museum's modern textbook, all shiny pages and timelines, and Ms. Charles had shaken her head at his draft.

"You need a primary source," she had said, and nothing more.

"That's the museum one," said Allegra, dropping onto the wall beside him with a granola bar. The wind off the memorial lawn smelled of cut grass and cold metal. "I did mine on the letters. A primary source is something made at the time by a person who lived through an event. Like my letters from the soldier."

"So the textbook doesn't count?"

"The textbook's written later, by someone studying it. That makes it a secondary source."

Cameron scrolled through the museum's digital collection and found a settler's diary, scanned page by page, the ink brown and spidery. He read it aloud while pigeons argued on the cannon nearby. "May the 14th. Rain again. Thomas says the land here is tired, and the soil in the west is black as coffee. We will follow the birds." He looked up. "Follow the birds?"

Eesa leaned over from the other side of the wall, where he had been copying names off the memorial into his notebook. "Migratory birds. They go west in spring, don't they? Maybe he watched which way the geese flew."

Cameron tested the idea. He flipped through the diary pages, hunting for the same pattern, and there it was again: a sketch of geese in a V, pointing west, and beside it, "good land lies where the birds rest." So the settler's motive wasn't just soil, it was the birds as a sign. He could eliminate the textbook now, cross it off his source list, because the diary was the thing made at the time by someone who lived through it. The textbook could still back him up later, but the diary was the heart of the argument.

He started his new draft right there, notebook on his knees, wind flapping the pages until Allegra pinned them down with her granola bar wrapper. "Paragraph one," he said, printing hard. "A settler's diary from the trail. Quote the geese."

Eesa peered over his shoulder. "Better than mine. I just have names."

"Yours matters too," Cameron said, and he meant it, then bent back over the page and wrote the first line in ink that wouldn't blow away: The birds knew the way before the people did.

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: When the price of one good rises, many buyers switch to a substitute, a similar good that does the same job, so demand for the substitute goes up.
story:
Juliette had five dollars and one plan: the glass prism on Mr. Byrne's folding table. She had seen it from the sidewalk, throwing a small rainbow onto the pavement when the sun hit it. By the time she crossed the lawn, a boy was already holding it up, turning it so the light refracted onto his shoe.

Mr. Byrne had penciled a new sign and clipped it to the front of the table. The old one, THREE DOLLARS, lay crumpled in the grass. The new one said EIGHT DOLLARS. "Three people asked for it in ten minutes," he told the boy. "Only one like it here." Juliette looked down the table. There were four boxes of paperbacks, a bucket of spoons, and one bowl of heavy glass doorknobs, marked fifty cents each. She had five dollars. The prism was out of reach unless the boy walked away, and he was counting out eight ones.

Behind her, Malia was working a card table with a pitcher of lemonade and a sign that said TWO DOLLARS A CUP. Two kids looked at the sign, looked at their single dollars, and drifted next door, where Anaya stood beside her own pitcher, handwritten sign reading ICED TEA, ONE DOLLAR. Anaya poured cup after cup. "Tea's basically a substitute," Malia said, arms crossed. "Same job on a hot day, half the price." By eleven o'clock Anaya's pitcher was empty and a line of kids stood in front of her, waiting for her mother to carry out the backup jug from the kitchen. Malia stared at her own full pitcher, then got a marker and scratched out the two.

Juliette watched all of it and turned back to Mr. Byrne's table with a new idea. The prism's price had jumped because everyone wanted the one fancy thing. But the doorknobs would do the same job, splitting sunlight into color. She picked one up, held it to the sun, and got a wobbly rainbow across the paperbacks. It worked. Not as sharp, but it worked. She put two more in her hand and brought all three to Mr. Byrne.

"Fifty cents each," he said, reading his own sign. Then he paused, because the boy with the prism was gone and two girls from the line at Anaya's table had wandered over. One of them pointed at the bowl of doorknobs and asked what they cost. Mr. Byrne looked at the empty spot where the prism had been, then at the bowl, and said, "A dollar each now." Juliette set her three down on the scale. "You said fifty. I picked these out before she came over." He rubbed the pencil mark on the sign, seemed to consider, and said, "Fair enough. Fifty for you. Dollar for everybody after."

She paid a dollar and fifty and carried the doorknobs home in her backpack just as the clouds stacked up, heavy and green like a monsoon sky. On her front steps she lined them up along the railing and waited for a break in the light. When the sun cut through, three crooked rainbows fell across the porch boards. Malia came up the walk with her pitcher, still unsold, and stopped to look. "Okay," Malia said. "I'm dropping my price to a dollar before the weekend. And I'm buying one of those."

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: Professional fact-checkers use lateral reading: instead of judging a website by its own pages, they open new tabs to see what other sources say about it.
story:
Blaine's basement smelled like popcorn, and his laptop glowed on the ping-pong table between them. Kenan leaned in from the other side.

"See?" Blaine said, turning the screen around. "VelocityWater dot com. It says professional athletes drink it and their injuries heal in half the time. My cousin wants me to buy a case with my birthday money."

The website really did look impressive. There were photographs of runners, a video with dramatic music, and a quote from somebody called Dr. Harlan Voss. "It seems real," Rachel admitted. She scrolled through the About page, and everything there was polished too, which almost convinced her.

Then she stopped. Something about it felt like the time her neighbour Mr. Rao had shown her a flyer for a roofing company that vanished after one storm. She opened a new tab and typed the company's name into a search. In another tab, she searched for "Dr. Harlan Voss." The results were strange. Nobody outside the website mentioned him at all. Then she found a news article from two years earlier: the company selling the drink had been warned for making up health claims. The whole amazing website, every last page of it, was run by the people profiting from it.

"It's like checking what other people say about somebody instead of just asking the person themselves," Rachel said slowly. Kenan nodded. "Mr. Rao calls that lateral reading. He does it before he trusts any website about mortgage rates, since scam sites love that topic." Blaine typed it into his notes.

"My cousin's going to say the website looks so professional," Blaine said.

"Then show him what you found in the other tabs," Rachel said. She scrolled back to the news article, where a lawyer had called the company negligent for ignoring safety warnings, and a reporter described how their fake review pages had been thwarted by a regulator who demanded they publish a correction. "It's all right here."

Blaine copied the link and texted it to his cousin. Then he closed the laptop halfway, like he was shutting a door on a salesman.

"He already answered," Blaine said, holding up his phone. "He says thanks, and he's buying a water filter instead."

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
knowledge_domain: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
fact: Chocolate contains theobromine, which dogs break down very slowly, and dark or baking chocolate is far more dangerous to them than milk chocolate.
story:
Levi carried the cardboard box the whole six blocks home, even though his arms ached, because the puppy inside kept trying to climb out. His neighbor Mr. Ortiz had found the litter behind his garage, and after a week of posted signs nobody claimed the wriggling brown one with the white sock feet. "He's yours now," Mr. Ortiz had said, and those words had propelled Levi down the sidewalk faster than his bike ever had. The puppy, who he was calling Biscuit, rode home quietly for once, watching the houses slide past.

Levi set the box on the kitchen counter only long enough to grab the water bowl from under the sink, and that was his mistake. When he turned back, Biscuit had tipped out of the box, landed on the counter somehow, and was chewing through a plastic bag with his whole face buried in it. The bag was the dark baking chocolate his mom used for cookies. Half a square was already gone. "No, drop it," Levi said, and Biscuit dropped it and wagged, thrilled by the new game.

Levi's stomach went cold. He had read one thing about dogs, on a flyer at the pet store, and it had said something about chocolate being bad. But he'd also seen Ryleigh's lab eat a dropped M&M at the park and be fine, so maybe it was all exaggeration. Then he remembered the flyer's exact words, which he'd thought were weird at the time: dogs break down the stuff in chocolate, which was called theobromine, very slowly, so it stays in them. And dark chocolate and baking chocolate were far more dangerous than milk chocolate, because they had more of it. Biscuit had just eaten baking chocolate. The M&M hadn't mattered. This did.

He tested his reasoning out loud, walking in a circle. "Milk chocolate, small amount, fine. Baking chocolate, half a square, not fine." He called Ryleigh to check, and Kurtis was there too, since they'd been planning to come see the puppy. "Yeah, my aunt's dog got into cocoa powder once," Ryleigh said. "They called the vet right away. The vet said the dark stuff is the dangerous stuff." Kurtis added, "It's called theobromine, that's what the vet said it's called." Levi hung up and dialed the vet's number with shaking fingers, and a calm voice on the line asked how much, what kind, and how much the puppy weighed. "Bring him in now," she said.

At the clinic, they took Biscuit through a door Levi couldn't follow him through, and he sat in the waiting room gripping the empty chocolate bag like it was evidence. Forty minutes later a tech carried Biscuit out, sleepy but walking on his own four sock feet, and said he'd be stable and fine by morning. Levi held him against his chest all the way home, and at the counter he swept every bag of chocolate into the highest cabinet, then pushed the box of dog biscuits to the front where Biscuit could see them. "Yours," he said. "The chocolate is mine."

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: The treble clef is also called the G clef because its curl circles the staff line for the note G.
story:
Grandpa's trumpet sat on the piano bench like it had been waiting for Joshua all summer. He lifted it, turned it in the light, and blew until his lips buzzed and a wobbly note finally squeaked out. He wanted to be ready for band tryouts in September, and Grandpa had promised to teach him everything.

"First you read music," Grandpa said, sliding a beginners book across the piano. "Start with this page." Joshua stared at the five lines, the black dots, and the swirly symbol at the start that looked like a fancy ampersand. Every time he tried to name a note, he guessed. G? C? He couldn't tell, and guessing wouldn't cut it when the band director handed out real music.

Then he noticed something. The swirl at the beginning of the staff curled around one line and circled it, like a lasso. He traced it with his finger, again and again. The second line from the bottom. What if the swirl was pointing to a specific note on purpose? He counted up from the bottom line, then dug out the little chart taped inside the book cover. The second line was G. The swirl circled G. "Grandpa, is that why they call it the G clef?" he asked. Grandpa grinned and said, "That's exactly why, the treble clef is the G clef." From that moment, Joshua could find G anywhere on the page, and he climbed the alphabet from there, naming notes faster and faster until the lines stopped being a mess and started being a map.

Agam came over the next day, skeptical as usual. "You learned to read music in one afternoon? Sounds like propaganda to make me feel slow." Joshua slid the book across the porch steps. "Count up to the second line and tell me what you see." Agam traced the curl, checked the chart, and his eyebrows went up. "It circles G. Every single time." He'd been sure it was luck, but now he couldn't refute it; the pattern held on every page, every song.

Mr. Brennan, the neighbor, heard them practicing on the porch and wandered over with his coffee. "Explicit instructions from the swirl itself," he said, tapping the page. "Can't argue with that." Joshua raised the trumpet, found his note, and blew a clean, round G that rang out across the yard.

activity: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale
knowledge_domain: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale
fact: Baking soda dissolved in water makes a mildly basic solution, with a pH of about 8 to 9.
story:
Bentley had turned his dad's garage into a lab, which mostly meant dragging a card table next to the lawnmower and taping a hand-lettered sign to it that said SCIENCE. Sahil and Sara sat on overturned buckets while Bentley lined up six clear cups. "Today we test acids and bases," he announced. "Mr. Shin gave me litmus paper from his hardware shop. Blue paper turns red in acid, and red paper turns blue in base."

"If it's neutral, nothing happens," Sara said. "Like plain water. Water's neutral, pH 7."

"Exactly." Bentley dropped a strip of blue paper into the vinegar cup and they watched it flush pink. Lemon juice did the same. Sara contributed a splash of her mom's leftover coffee, which turned the paper a distinct brick red, darker than the vinegar had. Sahil wrote it all down in a notebook, frowning at his own spelling of "phenomenon."

Then Bentley stirred a spoonful of baking soda into a cup of water. "This one's easy," he said, feeling smug. "Baking soda in water. It's basically just water with powder in it. I'd say the probability of it testing neutral is about a hundred percent." He dipped the red paper in and waited for nothing to happen.

The paper turned blue.

"That's not nothing," Sahil said. "That's very much something."

Bentley leaned over the cup like it might confess. He dipped the blue paper in too, and it stayed blue, calm as anything. "So it's not acid," he said slowly, thinking out loud, "because acid would have turned the blue paper red. It's a base. The baking soda did that. Baking soda dissolved in water makes a mildly basic solution." He fished out the box and squinted at it as if it had been keeping a secret from him all along. "Powdered betrayal," he muttered, and Sara laughed so hard she nearly fell off her bucket.

They ran the test three more times, and every strip came back blue. Sara checked a chart on Bentley's notebook cover and held it up. "Mildly basic, it says, pH of about 8 to 9." Bentley exhaled, long and dramatic, and wrote the numbers in Sahil's notebook in his biggest handwriting. Then he uncapped the vinegar and, with great ceremony, dripped it into the baking soda cup. The fizz climbed the side and overflowed onto the card table, and all three of them scrambled back, laughing, while the puddle hissed quietly between the battery charger and the lawnmower.

activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
knowledge_domain: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
fact: Answering an insult with another insult tends to escalate a situation, while a short, calm statement like "That's not funny, stop" gives nothing new to fight about.
story:
The bus jolted over the pothole by the elementary school, and Elliot had three stops left to figure out what to do about Karson. Every morning for a week, Karson had been calling Izaiah "Radio Tooth" because of the gap between his front teeth, and every morning Izaiah just stared out the window and took it. Yesterday, Izaiah had finally fired back with a clever comeback about Karson's haircut, and the whole back of the bus had howled. Elliot had expected that to end things. Instead Karson came back twice as mean, and by afternoon he had two other kids chanting the nickname too. Elliot turned that over all day. The comeback had been funny, but funny gave Karson something new to hit back at. It was like the teasing had its own hierarchy, and a punchy insult just moved Izaiah up to a bigger target.

Elliot had written a note during math and folded it into his pocket, and when Izaiah slid into the seat across the aisle, Elliot passed it over. The note said, "Meet me at the back before Karson gets on. I have an idea." Izaiah read it twice, gave a small nod, and moved.

Karson boarded at the corner by the pharmacy, loud from the first step. "Morning, Radio Tooth. You broadcasting today?"

Elliot's first try came out too abrupt, almost like a shove in words. "Karson, your haircut looks like a lawnmower lost a fight with you." Karson's grin got wider, not smaller, and Elliot felt his stomach drop. Wrong move. He could see it happening again, exactly like yesterday, the teasing inflating because he'd handed Karson fresh material.

He took a breath and tried the other direction. "That's not funny. Stop." Four words, flat and calm. Nothing in them to fight about.

Karson blinked. "What, are you his bodyguard now?"

"That's not funny. Stop," Elliot said again, same tone, and Izaiah, catching on, repeated it too. "Not funny. Stop."

Karson looked for a hook and found nothing to grab. He muttered something about boring people, put in his earbuds, and turned toward the window. The two chanting kids glanced at each other, uncertain now that there was no show.

At the next stop, after Karson shuffled down the steps without a single word about teeth, Izaiah leaned over. "Where'd you get that?"

"Figured it out after yesterday," Elliot said. He had almost confided the whole thing to Ms. Otieno after class, the note about Karson still crumpled in his pocket, but he'd wanted one more try on his own first. Now he was glad he'd waited.

"Same bus tomorrow?" Izaiah asked.

"Same seat," said Elliot, and pressed the note flat into his pocket.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Joining a club or team at a new school puts a student in regular contact with the same people who share an interest, which gives friendships time to grow.
story:
The movers carried the last box on Tuesday, and by Thursday Rebecca was standing in Room 12 with her schedule in her hand. She counted eleven desks before Mr. McKenzie called roll. At lunch she sat at the end of a table of girls who already knew one another's jokes, and by Friday she had learned exactly one name, and that was only because it was printed on a worksheet: Shyla.

At her old school it had taken her three weeks to become friends with the girl next door, and that was only because they kept meeting at the same bus stop every morning. Rebecca wrote this down in her notebook so she could see it: friends came from seeing the same people over and over. Random lunch tables didn't work because the people changed every day. She needed one place, one group, meeting regularly, so that a friendship would have time to grow, the way seeds needed a whole season. A class where everybody shared one interest would be even better, because then there would be something to talk about besides the weather.

She found the list of clubs taped beside the office: art, robotics, drama, chess. Chess met Tuesdays and Thursdays in Room 9. Her grandfather had taught her the game two summers ago, and she could still beat him about half the time. She wrote her name on the sign-up sheet.

On Tuesday, Room 9 held six kids and a folding table with three boards set up. A girl with short braids looked up. "I'm Ellie. You know the rules? I need a real opponent, everyone here plays wrong." Ellie was entering the county tournament in November and couldn't practice properly against people who moved their knights sideways. Rebecca sat down and captured Ellie's bishop on the ninth move. Ellie stared at the board, then grinned. "Thursday. Same time. Don't forget."

They played again Thursday, and the Tuesday after that, and the one after that. Rebecca brought granola bars because Ellie claimed she played worse without carbohydrates in her system, and Ellie traded her a laminated sheet of openings she had copied from the library. Between games they argued about whether the knight or the bishop was worth more, and one afternoon Ellie mentioned that the club was exactly the reason she'd stopped eating lunch in the bathroom last year.

In November Rebecca rode with Ellie's mother to the tournament and sat in the third row during the final game. Ellie won on time, held the small plastic trophy over her head, and pointed straight at Rebecca from the stage. On the bus home, Ellie leaned against the window and said, "Next year we both enter." Rebecca looked out at the highway lights going by and said, "Okay. I'll document every game we play, so we can study them." She opened her notebook and started with the date.
